q-3435:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, the $-10z$ term to the left-hand side, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}-50 & =-10z \\ {z}^{2}+10z & =50 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot 5\cdot z & =50 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot 5\cdot z+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =50 \\ (z+5{)}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =50\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(z+5{)}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =50 \\ (z+5{)}^{2} & =75\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=5,q=75,$ and $p+q=80.$

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(z+5{)}^{2} & =75 \\ \sqrt{(z+5{)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{75} \\ |z+5| & =\sqrt{75} \\ z+5 & =\pm 5\sqrt{3} \\ z & =-5\pm 5\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

q-12995:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, the $-10z$ term to the left-hand side, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}-25 & =-10z \\ {z}^{2}+10z & =25 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot 5\cdot z & =25 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot 5\cdot z+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =25 \\ (z+5{)}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =25\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(z+5{)}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =25 \\ (z+5{)}^{2} & =50\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=5,q=50,$ and $p+q=55.$

q-66902:
First, we rearrange our equation into a form that is more convenient for logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5z}-6 & =-2 \\ {e}^{-5z} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation and solve for $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5z} & =4 \\ ln⁡({e}^{-5z}) & =ln⁡(4) \\ -5z & =ln⁡(4) \\ z & =-\frac{1}{5}ln⁡(4)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $z=-\frac{1}{5}ln⁡(4)$

Evaluating the above expression using a calculator gives

$$
z≈-0.277
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

q-69903:
In this case, we need to put the fractions over a common denominator of $3x(1+z),$ since there are no common factors in either denominator that we can exploit.

To do this, we multiply the top and bottom of the first fraction by $3$, and the top and bottom of the second fraction by $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{x(1+z)}+\frac{1}{3(1+z)} & = \\ \frac{3}{3}\cdot \frac{2}{x(1+z)}+\frac{x}{x}\cdot \frac{1}{3(1+z)} & = \\ \frac{6}{3x(1+z)}+\frac{x}{3x(1+z)} & = \\ \frac{6+x}{3x(1+z)} & \end{aligned}
$$

q-113217:
Using the fact that $3=\frac{3}{1},$ we can write the expression as

$$
\frac{3}{1}+\frac{5-p}{p}.
$$

 

In order to add the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. So, we put both fractions over a common denominator of $p$ by multiplying the top and bottom of the first fraction by $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{1}+\frac{5-p}{p} & = \\ \frac{p}{p}\cdot \frac{3}{1}+\frac{5-p}{p} & = \\ \frac{3p}{p}+\frac{5-p}{p}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we add the fractions and simplify the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3p}{p}+\frac{5-p}{p} & = \\ \frac{3p+5-p}{p} & = \\ \frac{2p+5}{p}\end{aligned}
$$

q-110042:
We have that the battery duration $L(t)$ is measured in hours and the charging time is measured in minutes. 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(t): & \text{hours} \\ t: & \text{minutes}\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative $\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}$ measures a change in $L(t)$ over a change in $t.$ So, it represents a ratio of the units:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}: & \frac{\text{hours}}{\text{minute}}\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, $\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}$ is measured in "hours per minute".

q-48611:
We have that the temperature $F(t)$ is measured in degrees Fahrenheit and the time is measured in minutes. 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t): & \text{degrees Fahrenheit} \\ t: & \text{minutes}\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative $\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t}$ measures a change in $F(t)$ over a change in $t.$ So, it represents a ratio of the units:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t}: & \frac{\text{degrees Fahrenheit}}{\text{minutes}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t}$ is measured in "degrees Fahrenheit per minute".

q-48684:
The function $A(b)$ gives the area of a rectangle with base $b.$ So

$$
{A}^{′}(b)=\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}b}=\frac{\text{Change in }A}{\text{Change in }b}.
$$

Therefore, ${A}^{′}(b)$ is the rate at which the area changes as the base changes.

q-72104:
The function $P(s)$ gives the perimeter of a pentagon with side $s.$ So,

$$
{P}^{′}(s)=\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}s}=\frac{\text{Change in }P}{\text{Change in }s}.
$$

Therefore, ${P}^{′}(s)$ is the rate at which the perimeter changes as each side changes.

q-48709:
The slope of the line tangent to the graph of $V(t)$ at $t=10$ gives the derivative of $V(t)$ at $t=10.$ So, we have that

$$
{V}^{′}(10)=1.5.
$$

We can interpret the above statement as

$\,$ *$10$ hours after launching, the number of visitors increased at a rate of $1\,500$ visitors per hour.*

q-48571:
The function ${U}^{′}(t)$ represents the rate at which the number of users is changing at the moment $t$ hours after launch. 

Therefore, ${U}^{′}(4)=650$ means:

$\,$ *$4$ hours after the launch, the number of users increased at a rate of $650$ users per hour*

q-112383:
Since we want to determine the rate of decrease in the amount of charge after $5$ hours, we have $t=5.$

Thus, the rate of decrease of the amount of charge after $5$ hours will be

$$
\begin{aligned}c(5) & =100\cdot {5}^{-0.2(5)} \\  & =100\cdot {5}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{100}{5} \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of decrease will be $20$ percent per hour.

q-48914:
The  rate of change in the number of elephants  $t$ years since $1990$ is equal to the difference between the two given rates, that is

$$
B(t)-D(t).
$$

As $1998$ is $8$ years after $1990$, we have $t=8.$  Hence, the  rate of change in the elephant population in that region in $1998$ was 

$$
\begin{aligned}B(8)-D(8) & =500\cdot {2}^{0.125(8)}-400\cdot {3}^{0.125(8)} \\  & =500\cdot 2-400\cdot 3 \\  & =-200.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change in the elephant population was $-200$ elephants per year.

q-72004:
The function $N(t)$ gives the number of bacteria inside the dish after $t$ hours. Then,

$$
{N}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}N(t)}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{Change in }N}{\text{Change in }t}.
$$

Thus, ${N}^{′}(t)$ gives the rate at which the number of bacteria is increasing at time $t$, which is the same as $r(t).$ Therefore, the relationship between $N(t)$ and $r(t)$ is ${N}^{′}(t)=r(t).$

q-72105:
The function $A(t)$ gives the altitude of the plane after $t$ hours. Then,

$$
{A}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}A(t)}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{Change in }A}{\text{Change in }t}.
$$

Thus, ${A}^{′}(t)$ gives the rate at which the altitude is increasing at time $t$, which is the same as $r(t).$ Therefore, the relationship between $A(t)$ and $r(t)$ is ${A}^{′}(t)=r(t).$

q-170494:
Let's plot $z$ in the complex plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13930486/assets/1bc5f38d44d9df32a7493f8d210bbc17d716d8a63316e3d730a1c4258d56fe46.png)

The complex number $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant of the complex plane. Therefore $\frac{3\pi }{2}<arg⁡(z)<2\pi .$ 

If $\alpha $ is the angle that $z$ makes with the positive real axis, then

$$
\alpha =arctan⁡(\frac{6}{9})=arctan⁡(\frac{2}{3})≈0.588\,00.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =arg⁡(z)=2\pi -0.588\,00≈5.70
$$

to two decimal places.
